claim: Many organisms, including species from all kingdoms of life, can survive desiccation by entering a state with no detectable metabolism.
source: Many organisms, including species from all kingdoms of life, can survive desiccation by entering a state with no detectable metabolism.
evidence: This is a general statement about anhydrobiosis that draws from established scientific knowledge about diverse organisms.

claim: C. elegans dauer larvae require elevated amounts of trehalose to survive desiccation.
source: To survive, C. elegans dauer larvae and stationary phase S. cerevisiae require elevated amounts of the disaccharide trehalose.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing trehalose accumulation and desiccation survival assays.

claim: Stationary phase S. cerevisiae require elevated amounts of trehalose to survive desiccation.
source: To survive, C. elegans dauer larvae and stationary phase S. cerevisiae require elevated amounts of the disaccharide trehalose.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing trehalose accumulation and desiccation survival assays in yeast.

claim: Dauer larvae and stationary phase yeast switch into a gluconeogenic mode in which metabolism is reoriented toward production of sugars from non-carbohydrate sources.
source: We found that dauer larvae and stationary phase yeast switched into a gluconeogenic mode in which metabolism was reoriented toward production of sugars from non-carbohydrate sources.
evidence: This is supported by metabolic labeling experiments and metabolite analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The gluconeogenic mode in dauer larvae and stationary phase yeast depends on full activity of the glyoxylate shunt.
source: This mode depended on full activity of the glyoxylate shunt (GS), which enables synthesis of trehalose from acetate.
evidence: This is supported by experiments comparing wild-type and GS-deficient mutants in both organisms.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt enables synthesis of trehalose from acetate.
source: This mode depended on full activity of the glyoxylate shunt (GS), which enables synthesis of trehalose from acetate.
evidence: This is supported by metabolic labeling experiments with 14C-acetate showing incorporation into trehalose.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt is especially critical during preparation of worms for harsh desiccation (preconditioning).
source: The GS was especially critical during preparation of worms for harsh desiccation (preconditioning) and during the entry of yeast into stationary phase.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced trehalose accumulation during preconditioning in GS-deficient worms.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt is especially critical during the entry of yeast into stationary phase.
source: The GS was especially critical during preparation of worms for harsh desiccation (preconditioning) and during the entry of yeast into stationary phase.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced trehalose and glycogen accumulation in GS-deficient yeast entering stationary phase.

claim: Loss of the glyoxylate shunt dramatically decreased desiccation tolerance in both C. elegans and S. cerevisiae.
source: Loss of the GS dramatically decreased desiccation tolerance in both organisms.
evidence: This is supported by desiccation survival assays showing reduced survival in GS-deficient mutants of both organisms.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt has a novel physiological role in desiccation tolerance.
source: Our results reveal a novel physiological role for the GS and elucidate a conserved metabolic rewiring that confers desiccation tolerance on organisms as diverse as worm and yeast.
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript and the lack of previously defined physiological roles for the GS.

claim: The metabolic rewiring involving the glyoxylate shunt is conserved between C. elegans and S. cerevisiae.
source: Our results reveal a novel physiological role for the GS and elucidate a conserved metabolic rewiring that confers desiccation tolerance on organisms as diverse as worm and yeast.
evidence: This is supported by parallel experimental findings in both organisms showing similar metabolic strategies.

claim: Anhydrobiosis is an ametabolic state in which organisms can persist in the absence of water for a long period of time.
source: To cope with this environmental insult, many organisms enter an ametabolic state known as anhydrobiosis (Keilin, 1959; Leprince and Buitink, 2015). In this state, organisms can persist in the absence of water for a long period of time; when water becomes available, they exit the anhydrobiotic state and fully resume their normal activities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on anhydrobiosis.

claim: C. elegans is an excellent anhydrobiote.
source: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans and the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae are excellent anhydrobiotes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and experimental data on C. elegans desiccation tolerance.

claim: S. cerevisiae is an excellent anhydrobiote.
source: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans and the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae are excellent anhydrobiotes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and experimental data on yeast desiccation tolerance.

claim: Trehalose biosynthesis and accumulation is a strategy for anhydrobiosis common to both worm and yeast.
source: One strategy for anhydrobiosis common to both worm and yeast is the biosynthesis and accumulation of trehalose (Erkut et al., 2011; Tapia and Koshland, 2014), a disaccharide made of two alpha-linked glucose moieties (Elbein, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data presented in this manuscript.

claim: Trehalose is a disaccharide made of two alpha-linked glucose moieties.
source: One strategy for anhydrobiosis common to both worm and yeast is the biosynthesis and accumulation of trehalose (Erkut et al., 2011; Tapia and Koshland, 2014), a disaccharide made of two alpha-linked glucose moieties (Elbein, 2003).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In C. elegans, trehalose preserves the native packing of membranes in the dried state.
source: In C. elegans, trehalose preserves the native packing of membranes in the dried state (Erkut et al., 2011; 2012) and stabilizes membranes against the adverse effects of fast rehydration (Abusharkh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Trehalose stabilizes membranes against the adverse effects of fast rehydration in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, trehalose preserves the native packing of membranes in the dried state (Erkut et al., 2011; 2012) and stabilizes membranes against the adverse effects of fast rehydration (Abusharkh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In yeast, trehalose functions as a long-lived chaperone, preventing protein aggregation upon desiccation.
source: In yeast, trehalose also functions as a long-lived chaperone, preventing protein aggregation upon desiccation (Tapia and Koshland, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Neither C. elegans nor S. cerevisiae invests in trehalose production during growth and development.
source: Neither C. elegans nor S. cerevisiae invests in trehalose production during growth and development.
evidence: This is supported by data showing low trehalose levels in L3 larvae and exponentially growing yeast.

claim: In the dauer larva of C. elegans, both species devote a substantial amount of their internal carbon reserve to trehalose biosynthesis.
source: By contrast, in their non-proliferative stages, i.e., the dauer larva in C. elegans (as shown in Penkov et al., 2015, and this study) and stationary phase in yeast (François and Parrou, 2001; Werner-Washburne et al., 1993), both species devote a substantial amount of their internal carbon reserve to trehalose biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by data in this study and citations to previous work.

claim: In stationary phase yeast, both species devote a substantial amount of their internal carbon reserve to trehalose biosynthesis.
source: By contrast, in their non-proliferative stages, i.e., the dauer larva in C. elegans (as shown in Penkov et al., 2015, and this study) and stationary phase in yeast (François and Parrou, 2001; Werner-Washburne et al., 1993), both species devote a substantial amount of their internal carbon reserve to trehalose biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The dauer larva is the only desiccation-tolerant stage of the C. elegans life cycle.
source: In the non-feeding dauer larva (the only desiccation-tolerant stage of the C. elegans life cycle), trehalose levels rise dramatically upon exposure to mild desiccation stress (preconditioning) (Erkut et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about C. elegans and citation to previous work.

claim: Trehalose levels rise dramatically in dauer larvae upon exposure to mild desiccation stress (preconditioning).
source: In the non-feeding dauer larva (the only desiccation-tolerant stage of the C. elegans life cycle), trehalose levels rise dramatically upon exposure to mild desiccation stress (preconditioning) (Erkut et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and data in this study.

claim: Stationary phase yeast cells accumulate trehalose.
source: Similarly, stationary phase yeast cells, which are tolerant to desiccation, also accumulate trehalose (Calahan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Stationary phase yeast cells are tolerant to desiccation.
source: Similarly, stationary phase yeast cells, which are tolerant to desiccation, also accumulate trehalose (Calahan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation and data in this study.

claim: Reproductive stage larvae of C. elegans feed on bacteria, from which they ingest mostly lipids and proteins, and to some extent sugars.
source: Reproductive stage larvae of C. elegans feed on bacteria, from which they ingest mostly lipids and proteins, and to some extent sugars; they assimilate these nutrients via glycolysis and/or the TCA cycle to produce energy (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about C. elegans feeding and metabolism, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Reproductive stage larvae of C. elegans assimilate nutrients via glycolysis and/or the TCA cycle to produce energy.
source: Reproductive stage larvae of C. elegans feed on bacteria, from which they ingest mostly lipids and proteins, and to some extent sugars; they assimilate these nutrients via glycolysis and/or the TCA cycle to produce energy (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about metabolism, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: When fed glucose, budding yeast grows exponentially and uses fermentative glycolysis for its energetic and biosynthetic needs.
source: On the other hand, when fed its preferred carbon source (glucose), budding yeast grows exponentially and uses fermentative glycolysis for its energetic and biosynthetic needs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast metabolism, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: During fermentative growth, yeast cells secrete ethanol as well as acetate.
source: Under these conditions, the cells secrete ethanol as well as acetate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast fermentative metabolism.

claim: As glucose is consumed and glucose concentrations drop, yeast cells undergo the diauxic shift, i.e., a transition to respiratory metabolism.
source: In yeast, as glucose is consumed and glucose concentrations drop, cells undergo the diauxic shift, i.e., a transition to respiratory metabolism (Schweizer and Dickinson, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Following the diauxic shift, yeast produce acetyl-CoA from accumulated ethanol, acetate, and glycerol.
source: Following this shift, yeast produce acetyl-CoA from accumulated ethanol, acetate, and glycerol, and switch to oxidative phosphorylation via the TCA cycle (Schweizer and Dickinson, 2004), which provides energy as well as precursor metabolites for amino acid biosynthesis and gluconeogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Following the diauxic shift, yeast switch to oxidative phosphorylation via the TCA cycle.
source: Following this shift, yeast produce acetyl-CoA from accumulated ethanol, acetate, and glycerol, and switch to oxidative phosphorylation via the TCA cycle (Schweizer and Dickinson, 2004), which provides energy as well as precursor metabolites for amino acid biosynthesis and gluconeogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The TCA cycle in yeast provides energy as well as precursor metabolites for amino acid biosynthesis and gluconeogenesis.
source: Following this shift, yeast produce acetyl-CoA from accumulated ethanol, acetate, and glycerol, and switch to oxidative phosphorylation via the TCA cycle (Schweizer and Dickinson, 2004), which provides energy as well as precursor metabolites for amino acid biosynthesis and gluconeogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the TCA cycle.

claim: In the stationary phase, yeast cells accumulate trehalose and glycogen.
source: Finally, in the stationary phase, yeast cells accumulate trehalose and glycogen (François and Parrou, 2001; Schweizer and Dickinson, 2004; Werner-Washburne et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data in this manuscript.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt is a shortcut in the TCA cycle.
source: The GS, a shortcut in the TCA cycle (Kornberg and Madsen, 1958), is conserved in bacteria (Kornberg, 1966), fungi (Lopez-Boado et al., 1988; Lorenz and Fink, 2001), protists (Levy and Scherbaum, 1965; Nakazawa et al., 2005), nematodes (Liu et al., 1995; Madin et al., 1985; Siddiqui et al., 2000), and plants (Eastmond and Graham, 2001; Kornberg and Beevers, 1957).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt is conserved in bacteria.
source: The GS, a shortcut in the TCA cycle (Kornberg and Madsen, 1958), is conserved in bacteria (Kornberg, 1966), fungi (Lopez-Boado et al., 1988; Lorenz and Fink, 2001), protists (Levy and Scherbaum, 1965; Nakazawa et al., 2005), nematodes (Liu et al., 1995; Madin et al., 1985; Siddiqui et al., 2000), and plants (Eastmond and Graham, 2001; Kornberg and Beevers, 1957).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt is conserved in fungi.
source: The GS, a shortcut in the TCA cycle (Kornberg and Madsen, 1958), is conserved in bacteria (Kornberg, 1966), fungi (Lopez-Boado et al., 1988; Lorenz and Fink, 2001), protists (Levy and Scherbaum, 1965; Nakazawa et al., 2005), nematodes (Liu et al., 1995; Madin et al., 1985; Siddiqui et al., 2000), and plants (Eastmond and Graham, 2001; Kornberg and Beevers, 1957).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt is conserved in protists.
source: The GS, a shortcut in the TCA cycle (Kornberg and Madsen, 1958), is conserved in bacteria (Kornberg, 1966), fungi (Lopez-Boado et al., 1988; Lorenz and Fink, 2001), protists (Levy and Scherbaum, 1965; Nakazawa et al., 2005), nematodes (Liu et al., 1995; Madin et al., 1985; Siddiqui et al., 2000), and plants (Eastmond and Graham, 2001; Kornberg and Beevers, 1957).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt is conserved in nematodes.
source: The GS, a shortcut in the TCA cycle (Kornberg and Madsen, 1958), is conserved in bacteria (Kornberg, 1966), fungi (Lopez-Boado et al., 1988; Lorenz and Fink, 2001), protists (Levy and Scherbaum, 1965; Nakazawa et al., 2005), nematodes (Liu et al., 1995; Madin et al., 1985; Siddiqui et al., 2000), and plants (Eastmond and Graham, 2001; Kornberg and Beevers, 1957).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt is conserved in plants.
source: The GS, a shortcut in the TCA cycle (Kornberg and Madsen, 1958), is conserved in bacteria (Kornberg, 1966), fungi (Lopez-Boado et al., 1988; Lorenz and Fink, 2001), protists (Levy and Scherbaum, 1965; Nakazawa et al., 2005), nematodes (Liu et al., 1995; Madin et al., 1985; Siddiqui et al., 2000), and plants (Eastmond and Graham, 2001; Kornberg and Beevers, 1957).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt bypasses two CO2-releasing steps of the TCA cycle to produce succinate.
source: It bypasses two CO2-releasing steps of the TCA cycle (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, reactions 3 and 4) to produce succinate, and incorporates an additional molecule of acetyl-CoA to form L-malate from glyoxylate (Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, reaction 10).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge illustrated in the figures.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt incorporates an additional molecule of acetyl-CoA to form L-malate from glyoxylate.
source: It bypasses two CO2-releasing steps of the TCA cycle (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, reactions 3 and 4) to produce succinate, and incorporates an additional molecule of acetyl-CoA to form L-malate from glyoxylate (Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, reaction 10).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge illustrated in the figures.

claim: Excess malate from the glyoxylate shunt can be converted into oxaloacetate and diverted into gluconeogenesis.
source: Instead of remaining within the TCA cycle, excess malate can be converted into oxaloacetate and diverted into gluconeogenesis (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, reaction 12) (Voet and Voet, 2010).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citation and illustrated in figures.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt serves as a prototypical anaplerotic pathway, leading to the accumulation of critical TCA cycle intermediates, particularly oxaloacetate.
source: Thus, the GS serves as a prototypical anaplerotic pathway, leading to the accumulation of critical TCA cycle intermediates, particularly oxaloacetate, which can be consumed for gluconeogenesis.
evidence: This is based on established biochemical knowledge about the glyoxylate shunt.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt generates less ATP and NADH than the TCA cycle.
source: Moreover, this pathway generates less ATP and NADH than the TCA cycle (Kornberg, 1966).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt has been studied in the context of microbial sporulation and growth.
source: The GS has primarily been studied in the context of microbial sporulation and growth (Kornberg and Krebs, 1957; Megraw and Beers, 1964), fungal virulence (Lorenz and Fink, 2001), and plant seed germination (Eastmond et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt has been studied in the context of fungal virulence.
source: The GS has primarily been studied in the context of microbial sporulation and growth (Kornberg and Krebs, 1957; Megraw and Beers, 1964), fungal virulence (Lorenz and Fink, 2001), and plant seed germination (Eastmond et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt has been studied in the context of plant seed germination.
source: The GS has primarily been studied in the context of microbial sporulation and growth (Kornberg and Krebs, 1957; Megraw and Beers, 1964), fungal virulence (Lorenz and Fink, 2001), and plant seed germination (Eastmond et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt is not physiologically essential to microbial sporulation, fungal virulence, or plant seed germination.
source: However, the GS is not physiologically essential to any of these processes (Voet and Voet, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: C. elegans has the full set of enzymes required for the glyoxylate shunt.
source: On the other hand, it is astonishing that C. elegans, a nematode and thus a member of the animal kingdom, has the full set of enzymes required for the GS (Liu et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt has been proposed to be involved in sugar homeostasis in C. elegans.
source: Although the GS has been proposed to be involved in sugar homeostasis in the worm (Frazier and Roth, 2009), its absence results in neither a detectable phenotype nor any effect on wild-type adult lifespan.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Absence of the glyoxylate shunt results in neither a detectable phenotype nor any effect on wild-type adult lifespan in C. elegans.
source: Although the GS has been proposed to be involved in sugar homeostasis in the worm (Frazier and Roth, 2009), its absence results in neither a detectable phenotype nor any effect on wild-type adult lifespan.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about GS mutants in C. elegans.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt may be required for the extended longevity of some mitochondrial mutants in C. elegans.
source: However, it may be required for the extended longevity of some mitochondrial mutants (Gallo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Dauer larvae consume approximately 5-fold less oxygen than L3 larvae.
source: In a given concentration of environmental oxygen, mitochondria of dauer larvae consumed ~5-fold less oxygen than those of L3 larvae (Figure 2A), indicating that dauer larvae exist in a hypoaerobic mode.
evidence: This is supported by oxygen consumption rate measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Dauer larvae exist in a hypoaerobic mode.
source: In a given concentration of environmental oxygen, mitochondria of dauer larvae consumed ~5-fold less oxygen than those of L3 larvae (Figure 2A), indicating that dauer larvae exist in a hypoaerobic mode.
evidence: This is inferred from the oxygen consumption data.

claim: Dauer larvae contain much less ATP than L3 larvae.
source: Moreover, dauer larvae contain much less ATP than L3 larvae (Penkov et al., 2015; Wadsworth and Riddle, 1989), indicating that they are also hypometabolic.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dauer larvae are hypometabolic.
source: Moreover, dauer larvae contain much less ATP than L3 larvae (Penkov et al., 2015; Wadsworth and Riddle, 1989), indicating that they are also hypometabolic.
evidence: This is inferred from ATP measurements.

claim: Non-feeding dauer larvae accumulate substantially larger amounts of trehalose than L3 larvae.
source: Next, we compared trehalose levels in L3 vs. non-feeding dauer larvae. The latter accumulated substantially larger amounts of trehalose (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by trehalose measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The aqueous phase of L3 extract contained many labeled compounds, including various amino acids.
source: The aqueous phase of L3 extract contained many labeled compounds, including various amino acids (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), but trehalose was not abundant (Figure 3A, spot 1).
evidence: This is supported by 2D-HPTLC analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Trehalose was not abundant in the aqueous phase of L3 extract.
source: The aqueous phase of L3 extract contained many labeled compounds, including various amino acids (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), but trehalose was not abundant (Figure 3A, spot 1).
evidence: This is supported by 2D-HPTLC analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In L3 larvae, the TCA cycle is mainly cataplerotic.
source: Thus, in this growth stage, the TCA cycle is mainly cataplerotic: in addition to reducing NAD+ and producing ATP, L3 larvae use intermediates to synthesize various building blocks such as amino acids, nucleotides, and sugars.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolite labeling patterns observed in L3 larvae.

claim: The aqueous fraction of dauer larvae contained only a limited number of metabolites, with trehalose being predominant.
source: By contrast, the aqueous fraction of dauer larvae contained only a limited number of metabolites, and fluorograms of this extract had one predominant spot, i.e., trehalose (Figure 3B, spot 1).
evidence: This is supported by 2D-HPTLC analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Metabolism in dauer larvae is almost entirely switched to a gluconeogenic mode in which sugars are produced by non-carbohydrate sources (acetate/fatty acids).
source: These data suggest that metabolism in dauer larvae is almost entirely switched to a gluconeogenic mode in which sugars are produced by non-carbohydrate sources (acetate/fatty acids).
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolite labeling patterns showing predominant trehalose synthesis from acetate.

claim: The amount of radioactivity incorporated into TAGs decreased substantially during preconditioning.
source: In the organic phase, the amount of radioactivity incorporated into TAGs decreased substantially during preconditioning (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by TLC analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Preconditioning dramatically increased the level of radioactively labeled trehalose in dauer larvae.
source: At the same time, preconditioning dramatically increased the level of radioactively labeled trehalose (Figure 3C, spot 1), and the amounts of glutamate and glutamine also increased (Figure 3C, spots 3 and 4, respectively; this observation is discussed later).
evidence: This is supported by 2D-HPTLC analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Preconditioning increased the amounts of glutamate and glutamine in dauer larvae.
source: At the same time, preconditioning dramatically increased the level of radioactively labeled trehalose (Figure 3C, spot 1), and the amounts of glutamate and glutamine also increased (Figure 3C, spots 3 and 4, respectively; this observation is discussed later).
evidence: This is supported by 2D-HPTLC analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The dauer larva takes advantage of its gluconeogenic mode to boost trehalose synthesis upon desiccation stress.
source: These results suggest that the dauer larva takes advantage of its gluconeogenic mode to boost trehalose synthesis upon desiccation stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolite labeling data showing increased trehalose synthesis during preconditioning.

claim: Transcripts encoding enzymes required for gluconeogenesis (mdh-1, mdh-2, and pck-2) were expressed at relatively high levels in dauer larvae even before preconditioning.
source: Transcripts encoding enzymes required for gluconeogenesis, mdh-1, mdh-2, and pck-2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, enzymes 9 and 12), were expressed at relatively high levels in dauer larvae even before preconditioning.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: mdh-1 (cytosolic malate dehydrogenase) and pck-2 (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase) were significantly upregulated during preconditioning.
source: Moreover, mdh-1 (cytosolic malate dehydrogenase) and pck-2 (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase), both of which are crucial for gluconeogenesis, were significantly upregulated during preconditioning, consistent with the increase in gluconeogenesis and sugar accumulation observed in the dauer larva.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome data.

claim: In C. elegans, isocitrate lyase and malate synthase are combined in one protein, ICL-1.
source: In C. elegans, these two enzymes are combined in one protein, ICL-1 (formerly known as GEI-7), which has both isocitrate lyase and malate synthase domains, and can thus carry out both reactions (Liu et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The deletion in the icl-1(ok531) allele introduces a frame-shift and an early stop codon (A373*), which should completely inactivate the glyoxylate shunt.
source: The deletion in the icl-1(ok531) allele introduces a frame-shift and an early stop codon (A373*), which should completely inactivate the GS strains harboring this mutation.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of how frameshift mutations affect protein function.

claim: The dauer and L3 larvae of daf-2;icl-1 exhibited no difference in respiration rate compared to daf-2.
source: Compared to daf-2, the dauer and L3 larvae of daf-2;icl-1 exhibited no difference in respiration rate (Figure 2A) or basal trehalose levels (Figure 2B), indicating that the GS has no influence on oxygen consumption or basal gluconeogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by oxygen consumption measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The dauer and L3 larvae of daf-2;icl-1 exhibited no difference in basal trehalose levels compared to daf-2.
source: Compared to daf-2, the dauer and L3 larvae of daf-2;icl-1 exhibited no difference in respiration rate (Figure 2A) or basal trehalose levels (Figure 2B), indicating that the GS has no influence on oxygen consumption or basal gluconeogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by trehalose measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt has no influence on oxygen consumption or basal gluconeogenesis in C. elegans.
source: Compared to daf-2, the dauer and L3 larvae of daf-2;icl-1 exhibited no difference in respiration rate (Figure 2A) or basal trehalose levels (Figure 2B), indicating that the GS has no influence on oxygen consumption or basal gluconeogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of differences in respiration and basal trehalose between wild-type and GS-deficient worms.

claim: The total trehalose level in daf-2 dauer larvae was approximately 100 µg trehalose/mg protein at baseline, and increased approximately 5-fold upon preconditioning.
source: Similar to our previous findings (Erkut et al., 2011), the total trehalose level in daf-2 dauer larvae was ~100 µg trehalose/mg protein at baseline, and increased ~5-fold upon preconditioning (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is supported by trehalose measurements shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: In daf-2;icl-1, the initial level of trehalose was the same as that of daf-2, but the increase upon preconditioning was only 2-fold.
source: In daf-2;icl-1, although the initial level of trehalose was the same as that of daf-2, the increase was only 2-fold (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is supported by trehalose measurements shown in Figure 3G and 3H.

claim: The major source of trehalose during preconditioning is the glyoxylate shunt.
source: This suggests that the major source of trehalose during preconditioning is the GS.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced trehalose accumulation in GS-deficient worms during preconditioning.

claim: Incorporation of radioactivity into trehalose was considerably reduced in daf-2;icl-1 relative to that in daf-2.
source: Incorporation of radioactivity into trehalose was considerably reduced in daf-2;icl-1 relative to that in daf-2 (compare Figure 3B and E).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of 2D-HPTLC fluorograms in Figures 3B and 3E.

claim: During preconditioning, radioactively labeled trehalose increased approximately 6-fold in daf-2, but only 2-fold in daf-2;icl-1.
source: Densitometry of fluorogram spots revealed that, during preconditioning, radioactively labeled trehalose increased ~6-fold in daf-2, but only 2-fold in daf-2;icl-1 (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by densitometry analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The average increase in labeled trehalose in daf-2 was larger than the increase in total (i.e., unlabeled) trehalose, suggesting preferential use of lipid sources for sugar production in this strain.
source: The average increase in labeled trehalose in daf-2 was larger than the increase in total (i.e., unlabeled) trehalose (Figure 3H), suggesting preferential use of lipid sources for sugar production in this strain.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of labeled and unlabeled trehalose increases.

claim: In daf-2;icl-1, the levels of total and labeled trehalose increased to similar extents.
source: By contrast, in daf-2;icl-1, the levels of total and labeled trehalose increased to similar extents.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The trehalose 6-phosphate synthase activity of daf-2 is not higher than that of daf-2;icl-1.
source: These differences in trehalose induction levels between daf-2 and daf-2;icl-1 cannot be assigned to the trehalose biosynthetic pathway because the trehalose 6-phosphate synthase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, reaction 25) activity of daf-2 is not higher than that of daf-2;icl-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by TPS activity measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The utilization of acetate (and thus fatty acids) for gluconeogenesis and trehalose biosynthesis depends on the existence of a functional glyoxylate shunt.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the utilization of acetate (and thus fatty acids) for gluconeogenesis and trehalose biosynthesis depends on the existence of a functional GS.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolic labeling experiments showing reduced incorporation of acetate into trehalose in GS-deficient worms.

claim: All strains (daf-2, daf-2;icl-1, and daf-2;∆∆tps) were equally tolerant to mild desiccation at 98% RH.
source: The desiccation survival assay revealed that all strains were equally tolerant to mild desiccation at 98% RH (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: daf-2;icl-1 was much more sensitive to harsh desiccation than daf-2, and exhibited very poor survival under those conditions.
source: However, daf-2;icl-1 was much more sensitive to harsh desiccation than daf-2, and exhibited very poor survival under those conditions (Figure 4B), although it was significantly more tolerant than daf-2;∆∆tps (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: daf-2;icl-1 was significantly more tolerant to harsh desiccation than daf-2;∆∆tps.
source: However, daf-2;icl-1 was much more sensitive to harsh desiccation than daf-2, and exhibited very poor survival under those conditions (Figure 4B), although it was significantly more tolerant than daf-2;∆∆tps (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A threshold level of trehalose must be reached during preconditioning in order for the worm to survive harsh desiccation.
source: These results suggest that a threshold level of trehalose must be reached during preconditioning in order for the worm to survive harsh desiccation.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between trehalose levels and desiccation survival.

claim: Both daf-2 and daf-2;icl-1 dauer larvae survived at least 16 hr of heat shock at 30 or 32°C.
source: Both daf-2 and daf-2;icl-1 dauer larvae survived at least 16 hr of heat shock at 30 or 32°C (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by heat shock survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 34°C, survival of daf-2 and daf-2;icl-1 dauer larvae dropped dramatically after 12 hr, with no dependence on strain.
source: At 34°C, survival dropped dramatically after 12 hr, with no dependence on strain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by heat shock survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Heat shock at 37°C could only be tolerated for 4 hr by daf-2 and daf-2;icl-1 dauer larvae, independent of the status of the glyoxylate shunt.
source: Finally, heat shock at 37°C could only be tolerated for 4 hr, again independent of the status of the GS shunt (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by heat shock survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt is specifically involved in tolerance of desiccation, and possibly related stresses, in C. elegans.
source: These results suggest that the GS is specifically involved in tolerance of desiccation, and possibly related stresses, in C. elegans.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of GS deficiency on heat shock tolerance but strong effect on desiccation tolerance.

claim: The C. elegans ICL-1 protein sequence has a 20 amino acid N-terminal mitochondrial import sequence (MSSAAKNFYQVVKSAPKGRF).
source: Using a bioinformatics tool (Claros and Vincens, 1996), we analyzed the C. elegans ICL-1 protein sequence. We identified a 20 amino acid N-terminal mitochondrial import sequence (MSSAAKNFYQVVKSAPKGRF) and calculated an 88% probability that the protein is imported into mitochondria.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatics analysis using MitoProt.

claim: There is an 88% probability that C. elegans ICL-1 is imported into mitochondria.
source: Using a bioinformatics tool (Claros and Vincens, 1996), we analyzed the C. elegans ICL-1 protein sequence. We identified a 20 amino acid N-terminal mitochondrial import sequence (MSSAAKNFYQVVKSAPKGRF) and calculated an 88% probability that the protein is imported into mitochondria.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatics analysis using MitoProt.

claim: ICL-1::GFP was expressed at the highest levels in hypodermal cells in L3 larvae.
source: We first analyzed the localization of ICL-1::GFP in reproductive stage, actively feeding L3 larva. The protein was expressed at the highest levels in hypodermal cells (Figure 5A), although strong expression was also detected in the pharynx (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and gut (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ICL-1::GFP was also expressed in the pharynx and gut of L3 larvae.
source: We first analyzed the localization of ICL-1::GFP in reproductive stage, actively feeding L3 larva. The protein was expressed at the highest levels in hypodermal cells (Figure 5A), although strong expression was also detected in the pharynx (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and gut (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: In hypodermal syncytium, ICL-1::GFP was present in a tubular network interspersed with spherical structures, resembling mitochondrial staining of C. elegans.
source: In hypodermal syncytium, the protein was present in a tubular network interspersed with spherical structures (Figure 5A), resembling mitochondrial staining of C. elegans (Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 5A and comparison to known mitochondrial staining patterns.

claim: In hypodermal cells expressing ICL-1, the MitoTracker and GFP signals fully overlapped.
source: In hypodermal cells expressing ICL-1, the MitoTracker and GFP signals fully overlapped, whereas seam cells did not express ICL-1 at all (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization microscopy shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Seam cells did not express ICL-1.
source: In hypodermal cells expressing ICL-1, the MitoTracker and GFP signals fully overlapped, whereas seam cells did not express ICL-1 at all (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 5C.

claim: TPS-1 is almost exclusively localized to hypodermis and is not expressed in seam cells.
source: It should be noted that TPS-1, the key enzyme in trehalose biosynthesis, is almost exclusively localized to hypodermis and is not expressed in seam cells (Penkov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: C. elegans ICL-1 is mitochondrial.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that C. elegans ICL-1 is mitochondrial, and suggest that in the worm, the GS occurs within or in association with mitochondria.
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data with MitoTracker.

claim: In C. elegans, the glyoxylate shunt occurs within or in association with mitochondria.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that C. elegans ICL-1 is mitochondrial, and suggest that in the worm, the GS occurs within or in association with mitochondria.
evidence: This is inferred from the mitochondrial localization of ICL-1.

claim: In the presence of glucose, yeast uses fermentative glycolysis during rapid proliferation, and under these conditions, very little trehalose accumulates.
source: In the presence of its preferred carbon source (glucose), yeast uses fermentative glycolysis during rapid proliferation (Figure 1B); under these conditions, very little trehalose accumulates (Tapia and Koshland, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Once glucose concentration falls, yeast cells undergo a diauxic shift, thereafter using aerobic respiration for their energetic needs in order to continue proliferation.
source: However, once glucose concentration falls, the cells undergo a diauxic shift, thereafter using aerobic respiration for their energetic needs in order to continue proliferation (Figures 1D, 6A); eventually, as external energy sources are depleted, the cells enter stationary phase.
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated in Figures 1D and 6A.

claim: As external energy sources are depleted, yeast cells enter stationary phase.
source: However, once glucose concentration falls, the cells undergo a diauxic shift, thereafter using aerobic respiration for their energetic needs in order to continue proliferation (Figures 1D, 6A); eventually, as external energy sources are depleted, the cells enter stationary phase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast growth.

claim: Although both glycolytic and respiratory activities are low in stationary phase yeast, the cells continue to accumulate trehalose and glycogen, which ultimately constitute >30% of total cell mass.
source: Although both glycolytic and respiratory activities are low in stationary phase, the cells continue to accumulate trehalose and glycogen, which ultimately constitute >30% of total cell mass (François and Parrou, 2001; Werner-Washburne et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In yeast, the glyoxylate shunt is carried out by isocitrate lyase, Icl1p.
source: In yeast, the GS is carried out by isocitrate lyase, Icl1p (Fernandez et al., 1992), and the malate synthases, primarily Mls1p but also Dal7p (Hartig et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In yeast, the glyoxylate shunt is carried out by the malate synthases, primarily Mls1p but also Dal7p.
source: In yeast, the GS is carried out by isocitrate lyase, Icl1p (Fernandez et al., 1992), and the malate synthases, primarily Mls1p but also Dal7p (Hartig et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: GS mutants exhibited no significant growth defect when grown in high glucose, irrespective of the presence or absence of amino acids.
source: As expected, GS mutants exhibited no significant growth defect when grown in high glucose, irrespective of the presence or absence of amino acids (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: When grown in high ethanol, GS mutants grew normally in YP medium, but their growth was impaired in minimal medium (S min) lacking free amino acids.
source: By contrast, when grown in high ethanol, GS mutants grew normally in YP medium, but their growth was impaired in minimal medium (S min) lacking free amino acids (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Free amino acids can feed into carbon consumption in the TCA cycle in yeast.
source: This suggests that free amino acids can feed into carbon consumption in the TCA cycle, as C. elegans, and that in the absence of free amino acids, the GS plays an important role in carbon metabolism.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth differences in the presence and absence of amino acids.

claim: In the absence of free amino acids, the glyoxylate shunt plays an important role in carbon metabolism in yeast.
source: This suggests that free amino acids can feed into carbon consumption in the TCA cycle, as C. elegans, and that in the absence of free amino acids, the GS plays an important role in carbon metabolism.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth impairment of GS mutants in minimal medium.

claim: When grown on acetate as the sole carbon source, GS mutants grew very poorly regardless of the availability of free amino acids.
source: Regardless of the availability of free amino acids, GS mutants grew very poorly under these conditions (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: When yeast are grown on acetate as the sole carbon source, they have high glyoxylate shunt activity and exhibit elevated TCA-independent acetate metabolism.
source: Under these conditions, yeast have high GS activity and exhibited elevated TCA-independent acetate metabolism (Lee et al., 2011; Schweizer and Dickinson, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In wild-type yeast cells grown in glucose, following the diauxic shift (20 hr) and in stationary phase (48 hr), cells accumulated considerable amounts of trehalose.
source: In cells grown in glucose, following the diauxic shift (20 hr, black bars) and in stationary phase (48 hr, grey bars), WT cells accumulated considerable amounts of trehalose (Figure 7A) and glycogen (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by trehalose measurements shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In wild-type yeast cells grown in glucose, following the diauxic shift (20 hr) and in stationary phase (48 hr), cells accumulated considerable amounts of glycogen.
source: In cells grown in glucose, following the diauxic shift (20 hr, black bars) and in stationary phase (48 hr, grey bars), WT cells accumulated considerable amounts of trehalose (Figure 7A) and glycogen (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by glycogen measurements shown in Figure 7C.

claim: GS-deficient yeast cells grown in glucose contained low (but detectable) amounts of trehalose, but no detectable glycogen stores.
source: By contrast, despite reaching high cell densities, GS-deficient cells contained low (but detectable) amounts of trehalose, but no detectable glycogen stores (Figure 7A,C) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by trehalose and glycogen measurements shown in Figures 7A and 7C.

claim: When grown with acetate as a carbon source, wild-type yeast cells showed even greater accumulation of trehalose and glycogen.
source: We also measured trehalose and glycogen in WT and GS-deficient cells grown with acetate as a carbon source. Under these conditions, we observed an even greater accumulation of trehalose and glycogen in WT cells, whereas GS-deficient cells contained low levels of trehalose and no detectable glycogen (Figure 7B,D).
evidence: This is supported by trehalose and glycogen measurements shown in Figures 7B and 7D.

claim: When grown with acetate as a carbon source, GS-deficient yeast cells contained low levels of trehalose and no detectable glycogen.
source: We also measured trehalose and glycogen in WT and GS-deficient cells grown with acetate as a carbon source. Under these conditions, we observed an even greater accumulation of trehalose and glycogen in WT cells, whereas GS-deficient cells contained low levels of trehalose and no detectable glycogen (Figure 7B,D).
evidence: This is supported by trehalose and glycogen measurements shown in Figures 7B and 7D.

claim: ∆tps1 yeast cells contained very low levels of trehalose, but high levels of glycogen.
source: As expected, ∆tps1 cells contained very low levels of trehalose, but high levels of glycogen, whereas ∆hsp104 cells had no defects in trehalose (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) or glycogen storage (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: ∆hsp104 yeast cells had no defects in trehalose or glycogen storage.
source: As expected, ∆tps1 cells contained very low levels of trehalose, but high levels of glycogen, whereas ∆hsp104 cells had no defects in trehalose (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) or glycogen storage (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: Tps1 and Tps2 amounts were unchanged in wild type and GS-deficient yeast cells.
source: We also measured Tps1 and Tps2 amounts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), which were unchanged in wild type and GS-deficient cells.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: S. cerevisiae cells rely on TCA cycle-independent acetyl-CoA consumption through the glyoxylate shunt to synthesize trehalose and glycogen.
source: Collectively, these data show that, much like preconditioned C. elegans dauer larvae, S. cerevisiae cells rely on TCA cycle-independent acetyl-CoA consumption through the GS to synthesize trehalose and glycogen.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced trehalose and glycogen in GS-deficient yeast.

claim: All yeast strains survived very well after 1 day of desiccation.
source: All strains survived very well after 1 day of desiccation (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by desiccation survival data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The viability of wild-type yeast cells remained high after 30 days of desiccation.
source: The viability of cells in WT cultures remained high after 30 days of desiccation (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by desiccation survival data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: ∆icl1, ∆icl1/∆tps1, and ∆icl1/∆hsp104 yeast cells exhibited very poor desiccation tolerance after 30 days, with viability at least 10-fold lower than that of WT cells.
source: By contrast, ∆icl1, ∆icl1/∆tps1, and ∆icl1/∆hsp104 cells exhibited very poor desiccation tolerance after 30 days, with viability at least 10-fold lower than that of WT cells and comparable to that of ∆tps1 cells lacking trehalose altogether (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by desiccation survival data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The viability of GS-deficient yeast after 30 days of desiccation was comparable to that of ∆tps1 cells lacking trehalose altogether.
source: By contrast, ∆icl1, ∆icl1/∆tps1, and ∆icl1/∆hsp104 cells exhibited very poor desiccation tolerance after 30 days, with viability at least 10-fold lower than that of WT cells and comparable to that of ∆tps1 cells lacking trehalose altogether (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by desiccation survival data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: ∆icl1 yeast cells supplemented with trehalose in the medium 24 hr before desiccation exhibited near-WT levels of desiccation tolerance.
source: Importantly, ∆icl1 cells supplemented with trehalose in the medium 24 hr before desiccation exhibited near-WT levels of desiccation tolerance (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by desiccation survival data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Wild type and GS-deficient yeast cells showed similar sensitivity to heat shock at 50°C.
source: We first tested the ability of S. cerevisiae cells to tolerate elevated temperatures, subjecting wild type or GS-deficient mutants to heat shock at 50°C either at different cell densities, or for increasing amounts of time (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C). Under both conditions, wild type as well as GS-deficient cells showed similar sensitivity to heat shock.
evidence: This is supported by heat shock survival data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: A considerable proportion of wild-type yeast cells survived even after six freeze-thaw cycles.
source: Although a considerable proportion of WT cells survived even after six freeze-thaw cycles, GS-deficient cells underwent a dramatic loss in viability after just two cycles (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by freeze-thaw survival data shown in Figure 8.

claim: GS-deficient yeast cells underwent a dramatic loss in viability after just two freeze-thaw cycles.
source: Although a considerable proportion of WT cells survived even after six freeze-thaw cycles, GS-deficient cells underwent a dramatic loss in viability after just two cycles (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by freeze-thaw survival data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt plays an essential role in yeast desiccation tolerance by promoting gluconeogenesis for the synthesis of trehalose.
source: Together, our observations demonstrate that the GS plays an essential role in yeast desiccation tolerance by promoting gluconeogenesis for the synthesis of trehalose.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on trehalose synthesis and desiccation survival in GS-deficient yeast.

claim: GS-dependent trehalose synthesis is critical for survival under conditions of other water-related stresses, such as freezing.
source: Our data also suggest that GS-dependent trehalose synthesis is critical for survival under conditions of other water-related stresses, such as freezing.
evidence: This is inferred from the freeze-thaw survival data.

claim: Dauer larvae exist in a hypometabolic state in which metabolism is redirected largely towards gluconeogenesis.
source: Here, we demonstrated that dauer larvae exist in a hypometabolic state in which metabolism is redirected largely towards gluconeogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by oxygen consumption, ATP measurements, and metabolite labeling data.

claim: The hypometabolic state of dauer larvae depends primarily on an active glyoxylate shunt.
source: This state depends primarily on an active glyoxylate shunt (GS), which serves as the main route for synthesis of trehalose from TAG reserves during preconditioning.
evidence: This is supported by metabolite labeling and trehalose accumulation data in GS-deficient worms.

claim: The glyoxylate shunt serves as the main route for synthesis of trehalose from TAG reserves during preconditioning in dauer larvae.
source: This state depends primarily on an active glyoxylate shunt (GS), which serves as the main route for synthesis of trehalose from TAG reserves during preconditioning.
evidence: This is supported by metabolite labeling experiments showing incorporation of acetate into trehalose.

claim: Budding yeast undergoes a conceptually convergent process to C. elegans for desiccation tolerance.
source: We also showed that budding yeast undergoes a conceptually convergent process.
evidence: This is inferred from the parallel findings in both organisms.

claim: In order to survive desiccation, stationary phase yeast cells must produce high levels of trehalose from acetate or glycerol.
source: In order to survive desiccation, stationary phase yeast cells must produce high levels of trehalose from acetate or glycerol.
evidence: This is supported by trehalose measurements and desiccation survival data in yeast.

claim: Conversion of acetate or glycerol to trehalose in yeast can be successfully accomplished only in the presence of a functional glyoxylate shunt.
source: This conversion can be successfully accomplished only in the presence of a functional GS.
evidence: This is supported by data showing reduced trehalose in GS-deficient yeast.

claim: Amino acids can be converted into their corresponding α-keto acids, which then undergo a specific series of reactions to enter the TCA cycle for gluconeogenesis.
source: Amino acids, for example, can be converted into their corresponding α-keto acids, which then undergo a specific series of reactions to enter the TCA cycle, in which they are subsequently used for gluconeogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Even via utilization of amino acids or other metabolites, daf-2;icl-1 dauer larvae cannot tolerate desiccation as well as daf-2.
source: However, even via utilization of amino acids or other metabolites, daf-2;icl-1 dauer larvae cannot tolerate desiccation as well as daf-2.
evidence: This is supported by desiccation survival data.

claim: An intermediate level of trehalose is insufficient for desiccation tolerance: Below some threshold level, trehalose cannot exert its protective effects and overcome the adverse consequences of desiccation.
source: Our data indicate that an intermediate level of trehalose is insufficient for desiccation tolerance: Below some threshold level, trehalose cannot exert its protective effects and overcome the adverse consequences of desiccation.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between trehalose levels and desiccation survival.

claim: A conceptually similar trehalose threshold may exist in C. elegans as has been explored in yeast.
source: This hypothesis was previously explored in yeast (Tapia et al., 2015). Our results strongly suggest that a conceptually similar trehalose threshold may exist in the worm as well.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and comparison to previous yeast studies.

claim: Gluconeogenesis is in general associated with the energetic needs of the organism.
source: It is worth to note that gluconeogenesis is in general associated with the energetic needs of the organism.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: In C. elegans and yeast, gluconeogenesis is additionally used as a defense against environmental stress.
source: In C. elegans and the yeast, however, it is additionally used as a defense against environmental stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing gluconeogenesis supporting trehalose synthesis for desiccation tolerance.

claim: Taking advantage of the glyoxylate shunt, worms and yeast devote large amounts of resources to the production of trehalose, which in turn protects the organism against desiccation or other water-related stresses, such as freezing and thawing during winter.
source: Taking advantage of the GS, worms and yeast devote large amounts of resources to the production of trehalose, which in turn protects the organism against desiccation or other water-related stresses, such as freezing and thawing during winter.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on trehalose synthesis, desiccation survival, and freeze-thaw survival.

claim: The germination of plant seeds was considered to be the most prominent process requiring the glyoxylate shunt.
source: For several decades, the germination of plant seeds was considered to be the most prominent process requiring this pathway, and it was assumed that production of sugars from seed oils was a prerequisite for germination.
evidence: This is based on historical scientific understanding.

claim: Studies of Arabidopsis lines with no functional glyoxylate shunt revealed that in the presence of light, this pathway is non-essential for seed germination.
source: However, studies of Arabidopsis lines with no functional GS revealed that in the presence of light, this pathway is non-essential (Eastmond et al., 2000; Eastmond and Graham, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: This study provides the first clearly defined physiological role for the glyoxylate shunt in C. elegans and S. cerevisiae.
source: To the best of our knowledge, our study provides the first clearly defined physiological role for the GS in C. elegans and S. cerevisiae.
evidence: This is based on the novel findings presented in the manuscript and the lack of previously defined physiological roles.

claim: One of the downstream effects of hygrosensation in C. elegans is likely to be increased lipolysis.
source: Although we still do not know the details of this sensation, one of its downstream effects is likely to be increased lipolysis.
evidence: This is speculated based on the need for acetyl-CoA from fatty acids to fuel the glyoxylate shunt.

claim: Lipolysis, followed by β-oxidation of fatty acids, yields acetyl-CoA, the fuel for the glyoxylate shunt.
source: This process, followed by β-oxidation of fatty acids, yields acetyl-CoA, the fuel for GS.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Lipolysis determines the extent of the glyoxylate shunt.
source: It is therefore reasonable to speculate that lipolysis determines the extent of the GS.
evidence: This is speculated based on the role of lipolysis in providing substrate for the glyoxylate shunt.

claim: ICL-1 is predominantly localized in the hypodermis of C. elegans.
source: As shown above, ICL-1 is predominantly localized in the hypodermis.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data.

claim: The major enzyme that synthesizes trehalose (TPS) is localized to the hypodermis in C. elegans.
source: The major enzyme that synthesizes trehalose (TPS) is localized to the same tissue (Penkov et al., 2015), but is not expressed in the gut.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The major TAG deposit in the form of fat droplets resides in the gut, and to some extent in the hypodermis of C. elegans.
source: On the other hand, the major TAG deposit in the form of fat droplets resides in the gut, and to some extent in the hypodermis (Mak, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Synthesis of trehalose in the hypodermis must depend on the transport of fatty acids from the gut.
source: Thus, synthesis of trehalose in the hypodermis must depend on the transport of fatty acids from the gut.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial separation of TAG stores and trehalose synthesis machinery.

claim: FAR-3 is strongly upregulated at both the transcriptional and translational levels upon preconditioning (~160 and four fold, respectively).
source: Indeed, as we previously found, one of the fatty acid-binding proteins (FAR-3) is strongly upregulated at both the transcriptional and translational levels upon preconditioning (~160 and four fold, respectively) (Erkut et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: FAR-3 is predicted to have a 20 amino acid signal sequence for secretion.
source: FAR-3 is predicted to have a 20 amino acid signal sequence for secretion, and could thus be involved in the transport of fatty acids between cells.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatics prediction.

claim: FAR-3 could be involved in the transport of fatty acids between cells.
source: FAR-3 is predicted to have a 20 amino acid signal sequence for secretion, and could thus be involved in the transport of fatty acids between cells.
evidence: This is speculated based on the predicted signal sequence and upregulation during preconditioning.

claim: The regulation of the glyoxylate shunt by substrate availability is a complex process that depends on interactions between different tissues.
source: These observations strongly suggest that the regulation of the GS by substrate availability is a complex process that depends on interactions between different tissues.
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific localization of ICL-1, TPS, and TAG stores.

claim: In plants and yeast, the glyoxylate shunt is split between mitochondria and a specialized organelle (glyoxysome or peroxisome) or the cytoplasm.
source: By contrast, in plants and the yeast, this pathway is split between mitochondria and a specialized organelle (glyoxysome or peroxisome) or the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the subcellular localization of the glyoxylate shunt in different organisms.

claim: In contrast to yeast and many other organisms, C. elegans ICL-1 is a bifunctional enzyme with both glyoxylase and malate synthase activities.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to yeast and many other organisms, C. elegans ICL-1 is a bifunctional enzyme with both glyoxylase and malate synthase activities.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on ICL-1.

claim: The differences in glyoxylate shunt organization between organisms suggest that transition into gluconeogenic mode is regulated differently in different organisms.
source: The physiological meaning of these differences remains elusive, but they suggest that transition into gluconeogenic mode is regulated differently in different organisms.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed differences in enzyme organization and localization.

claim: Loss of the glyoxylate shunt is deleterious during desiccation in both dauer larvae and stationary phase yeast.
source: In both species, loss of the GS is deleterious during desiccation.
evidence: This is supported by desiccation survival data in both organisms.

claim: The results reveal a novel physiological role for the glyoxylate shunt.
source: Our results reveal a novel physiological role for the GS and a conserved mechanism by which diverse organisms can regulate their metabolism to achieve desiccation tolerance.
evidence: This is based on the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The results reveal a conserved mechanism by which diverse organisms can regulate their metabolism to achieve desiccation tolerance.
source: Our results reveal a novel physiological role for the GS and a conserved mechanism by which diverse organisms can regulate their metabolism to achieve desiccation tolerance.
evidence: This is based on the parallel findings in C. elegans and S. cerevisiae.
